content: Central venous catheters are essential tools in the management of critically ill patients, as they facilitate both diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. These catheters are typically inserted into large veins such as the internal jugular vein in the neck, the subclavian vein in the upper chest, or the femoral vein in the groin. However, the procedure carries inherent risks, including arterial puncture and other complications, and should ideally be performed with minimal attempts to reduce these risks. Historically, clinicians relied on anatomical landmarks on the body surface to guide catheter placement. With advancements in technology, ultrasound imaging, including two-dimensional ultrasound and Doppler ultrasound, has become available to assist in this process. The primary aim of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of two-dimensional ultrasound (US) and Doppler ultrasound (USD) guidance compared to traditional anatomical landmark techniques for subclavian, axillary, and femoral vein catheterization in both adults and children. The review also sought to determine whether there were differences in complication rates between these methods. Secondary objectives included evaluating differences between US and USD techniques, comparing direct ultrasound guidance (used throughout the procedure) versus indirect guidance (used only to identify and mark the vein before the procedure), and assessing whether these differences varied based on patient groups or the experience level of the operator. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, up to January 2013, with an additional search in August 2014. The search also included grey literature, dissertations, and handsearching of intensive care and anesthesia journals, as well as conference proceedings. Efforts were made to identify unpublished or ongoing studies by contacting experts and companies in the field and searching trial registries. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared two-dimensional ultrasound or Doppler ultrasound guidance with anatomical landmark techniques for subclavian or femoral vein catheterization in adults and children. Data were independently extracted by three reviewers using a standardized form, and subgroup analyses were performed as planned. A total of 13 studies involving 2341 participants and 2360 procedures met the inclusion criteria. The quality of evidence varied, ranging from very low to high depending on the outcome and vein studied. For subclavian vein catheterization, two-dimensional ultrasound significantly reduced the risk of inadvertent arterial puncture (risk ratio [RR] 0.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.06 to 0.82; P = 0.02) and hematoma formation (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.76; P = 0.01). However, no significant differences were observed in overall complications, the number of attempts required for successful catheterization, first-attempt success rates, or the time taken to complete the procedure. For femoral vein catheterization, data were more limited. Ultrasound guidance increased the likelihood of success on the first attempt (RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.34 to 2.22; P < 0.0001) and showed a small improvement in overall success rates (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.23; P = 0.06). No significant differences were found in the rates of inadvertent arterial puncture or other complications. The studies did not report data on mortality or patient-reported outcomes. In conclusion, two-dimensional ultrasound guidance offers modest improvements in safety and procedural success compared to anatomical landmark techniques for subclavian and femoral vein catheterization. Specifically, it reduces the risk of arterial puncture and hematoma formation for subclavian vein access and increases first-attempt success rates for femoral vein access. However, evidence regarding the use of Doppler ultrasound, the impact of operator experience, and outcomes in high-risk patients remains uncertain.
